scenes.heading: Consistency Models
scenes.narration: A consistency model is the contract a distributed store makes about when and how writes become visible to readers, ranging from strict ordering to eventual convergence.

scenes.heading: A spectrum of guarantees
bullets: Strong: reads always see the latest committed write
Sequential and causal: preserve ordering of related ops
Eventual: replicas converge given enough time
scenes.narration: Strong consistency guarantees a read always reflects the latest committed write, as if there were one copy. Sequential and causal models relax this but still preserve the ordering of related operations. Session guarantees like read-your-writes and monotonic reads ensure a single client sees a sensible view even if the global picture lags. Eventual consistency promises only that, absent new writes, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value.

scenes.heading: Strong vs eventual
scenes.narration: Strong consistency is easy to reason about because every read sees the newest write, but it needs cross-node coordination that raises latency and can block during partitions, so it suits ledgers and inventory counts. Eventual consistency offers low latency and stays available under partitions, but it pushes the burden of conflict resolution onto the application and can surface stale data, which is acceptable for social feeds, like counts, and caches. Pick the weakest model your correctness requirements allow.

scenes.heading: Session guarantees users feel
bullets: Read-your-writes: see your own updates immediately
Monotonic reads: never see time go backwards
Monotonic writes: your writes apply in order
Consistent prefix: no gaps in the story
scenes.narration: Even under eventual consistency, session guarantees keep a single user's experience sane. Read-your-writes ensures you immediately see updates you just made, like an edited profile. Monotonic reads ensure that once you have seen a value, you never see an older one on a later read, so time does not appear to go backwards. Monotonic writes ensure your own writes are applied in the order you issued them. And consistent prefix reads ensure you see changes in a causally coherent order without confusing gaps.

scenes.heading: Tuning consistency with quorums
steps: Require W replicas to ack a write
Require R replicas to answer a read
If W plus R exceeds N, reads see latest
Lower W or R for speed, higher for safety
scenes.narration: Many stores let you tune consistency with quorums. You pick a replication factor N, the number of copies. A write must be acknowledged by W replicas, and a read must gather responses from R replicas. When W plus R is greater than N, the read and write sets overlap, guaranteeing a read sees the latest write. Lowering W or R favors speed and availability, while raising them favors consistency, so you dial the tradeoff per operation rather than for the whole system.

scenes.heading: How eventual convergence works
steps: Conflicts resolved by version or vector clock
scenes.narration: In an eventually consistent system a write lands on one replica, which acknowledges the client immediately for low latency. The change then propagates asynchronously to the other replicas. When concurrent writes collide, conflicts are resolved using version numbers, last-writer-wins timestamps, or vector clocks that track causality. Given a quiet period, every replica ends up holding the same value.

scenes.text: Consistency is a dial, not a switch; tune it per operation so critical paths stay strong while high-volume paths stay fast.
scenes.narration: Treat consistency as a dial rather than an on-off switch, tuning it per operation so that critical paths remain strongly consistent while high-volume, tolerant paths stay fast and available.
